# Space and cosmic scale: props in Line art

```
You are a senior prop designer. You are drawing the PROPS of one world for a code-rendered video engine
that makes workplace training and explainer videos for adults. They must match the sets of this world drawn in the
same style, and every prop must be a real, recognisable object built the way the real one is built.

FORMAT
- One SVG per prop, viewBox sized to the prop with 16 px of margin, the prop standing on its base line; mark the base
  with <circle id="anchor_base" r="2" fill="none"/> and any grip, screen or top with anchor_ circles.
- Groups: <g id="base"> for the shapes, and classed groups as in the set contract: lm-shadow (a contact shadow under
  the prop only), lm-light, lm-texture, lm-outline, lm-hi, lm-glow as the style uses them.
- Moving parts (a laptop lid, clock hands, a door, a drawer, a monitor arm) as their own groups with a pivot anchor.
- Views: front and three-quarter for furniture and devices; one view for small things.
- No text, letters, numbers or logos (slots as empty rects); no images, filters or masks; up to 120 KB per prop.

STYLE: LINE ART (for technical, minimal and elegant lessons; process and systems in a real place)
- An architect's interior drawing: precise two-point perspective and THREE line weights by depth, all in lm-outline: 3 px for the nearest and cut edges, 2 px for the middle ground, 1 px for the far ground. Single confident strokes; corners overlap very slightly rather than falling short.
- Fills only as the faint material tints of the palette on large planes (wall, floor, glass) so the drawing is not paper-white; no shading except a light hatch in the deepest corners.
- Detail hierarchy by line density: the focal area is drawn completely (chair mechanisms, table joints), the rest is drawn with fewer lines.
- Overlaps are shown by line breaks (a 4 px gap where a near line crosses a far one).
- Light: Implied only: the shadow side of each object gets the heavier line; cast shadows as an open hatch at 45 degrees in the shadow colour.
- Texture: None.
- Depth: Far: 1 px lines in the shadow colour instead of ink. Mid and near: ink.
- Quality bar: A presentation drawing from a good architecture practice: clean, exact, quietly beautiful.

THE WORLD: SPACE AND COSMIC SCALE
Earth's neighbourhood as one fictional international crewed space programme of the early 2030s sees it: the programme's flight control room on the ground, its laboratory module on a crewed station in low Earth orbit about 420 km up, the satellites that circle Earth (a satellite navigation constellation about 20,200 km up), and the Sun and planets around them. No real agency, mission, spacecraft or logo is drawn; Earth, the Moon, the Sun and the planets are the real ones, at their real sizes and colours whenever a scene states them.
Architecture:
- space itself: black, with sparse, small, faint stars (bright stars are few; a sunlit scene washes most of them out); no nebula clouds or coloured gas near Earth
- Earth from space: deep blue oceans, white cloud bands and spirals, brown and green land, a thin pale-blue line of atmosphere at the limb, city lights on the night side; a soft terminator between day and night
- satellites: small boxy bodies with two flat solar panel wings and a few antennas, a few metres across; navigation satellites circle about 20,200 km up on six rings tilted 55 degrees to the equator, four or more per ring
- the station module: a cylinder about 8.5 m long and 4.3 m across whose inside is lined on all four sides with equipment racks about 1.05 m wide, leaving a square aisle about 2.1 m high and wide; square hatches about 1.27 m at each end; handrails, foot loops, fastening patches, cable bundles and LED light panels along the corners
- the flight control room: a large, dim, flat-floored room about 20 by 16 m with four long rows of consoles (desks with two or three monitors per position, headsets, binders) facing a front wall of large screens set high enough to see over the monitors; dark acoustic walls and ceiling with small downlights
- the Sun and planets: the real bodies at their real relative sizes and colours (NASA planetary fact sheet)
Materials: in space: black sky, white and blue Earth, grey and gold satellites with dark-blue solar panels; in the station: off-white rack faces and fabric closeouts, grey fastening patches, aluminium handrails, black cable bundles, laptop screens; in the control room: dark grey acoustic panels, charcoal consoles with dark monitor backs, glowing screens. Palette families in this world (the set palette was named for rooms): the black of space is sky (its deep tone) and the station's and room's main surfaces are wall; screens that are off and monitor backs are screen; lit screens are paper hi with slots; Earth's oceans are glass, its land plant, its clouds paper; satellites and handrails are metal, their solar panels glass; the planets use the families nearest their real colours (Mars and Jupiter's spot brick, Saturn and Venus paper or brass, Uranus and Neptune glass); the Sun is light; warning lights are accent
Scale (draw to these real sizes; a person is about 1.75 m):
- Earth's radius is 6,371 km; the crewed station flies about 420 km up (1.07 Earth radii from the centre); navigation satellites about 20,200 km up (4.17 Earth radii from the centre); geostationary satellites about 35,786 km up (6.6 Earth radii)
- the Moon is 3,475 km across, about a quarter of Earth, and about 384,400 km away (60 Earth radii)
- planet diameters: Mercury 4,879 km, Venus 12,104, Earth 12,756, Mars 6,792, Jupiter 142,984, Saturn 120,536 (its main rings about 273,000 km across), Uranus 51,118, Neptune 49,528; the Sun 1,392,700 km (about 109 Earths)
- a person is about 1.75 m tall; the station's aisle is about 2.1 m square; a hatch about 1.27 m square; a station rack about 1.05 m wide
- a control room console desk is 0.75 m high with monitors to about 1.25 m; the front screens about 5.2 by 2.6 m, their bottoms 2.6 m above the floor
Signs of life (every set shows someone works here):
- the station is lived in: a tethered pen, a drink pouch stuck to a wall patch, a checklist clipped to a handrail, cargo bags strapped in place
- the control room is worked in: headsets left on monitors, an open procedures binder, a coffee cup, a jacket on a chair
- space is busy: satellites on their rings, the station's thin low orbit, the geostationary ring far out
- nothing floats loose in the station unless it is shown drifting on purpose
Default light: In space: hard, white sunlight from one side and black shadow on the other, with no air to soften it; Earth's day side bright and its night side dark with city lights. Inside the station: even, cool-white LED light from the panels along the corners. In the control room: dim, focused light from small downlights, with the screens glowing.
Outside: Seen from the station's window: Earth's curve, cloud and ocean; from the control room: nothing (it has no windows).
```
